questions.question: What is the role of a parity bit in an error-control code?
options: Add a constraint so some subsets have even/odd parity
Encrypt the data so flips become harmless
Compress the data so fewer bits can flip
Guarantee the channel never flips bits
questions.explanation: A parity bit is redundancy chosen so a subset of bits satisfies a parity constraint (even or odd).

questions.question: In Hamming codes, why are parity bits commonly placed at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, ...?
options: Their binary indices isolate which parity checks each bit participates in
It minimizes the number of 1s in the codeword
It makes the message bits always come first
It is required only for odd parity, not even parity
questions.explanation: Using power-of-two positions makes the parity coverage correspond to the bits of the position index, enabling syndrome-as-address decoding.

questions.question: For Hamming(7,4) with parity at positions 1,2,4, which positions hold data bits?
questions.explanation: Positions that are not powers of two are data positions: 3, 5, 6, and 7.

questions.question: What does it mean if the syndrome of a received 7-bit word is 000?
options: The word satisfies all parity checks (it is a valid codeword under the chosen convention)
The word must equal the original message bits
Exactly one bit was flipped and corrected
The decoder can safely assume there were two bit flips
questions.explanation: A zero syndrome means the received word satisfies the parity-check equations; it may still be wrong if more complex error patterns map to a valid codeword.

questions.question: If syndrome bits are ordered as [1,2,4] and the syndrome is [1,0,1], which 1-indexed position does it indicate?
In the layout [p1,p2,d1,p4,d2,d3,d4] with even parity, which equation correctly defines p4?
questions.explanation: p4 covers positions 4,5,6,7 (p4,d2,d3,d4), so for even parity p4 = d2 ⊕ d3 ⊕ d4.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what can happen if you apply single-error correction to a received word that actually has two flipped bits?
options: You can miscorrect into a different valid codeword and decode the wrong message
You will always detect the two-bit error and refuse to decode
You will always recover the original message anyway
The syndrome is guaranteed to be 000 for any two-bit error
questions.explanation: Plain Hamming(7,4) cannot reliably distinguish 1-bit from 2-bit errors; syndrome-based correction can silently produce the wrong valid codeword.

questions.question: A Hamming(7,4) code has minimum distance d_min = 3. What does that guarantee?
options: Correct up to 1 bit flip and detect up to 2 bit flips
Correct up to 2 bit flips and detect up to 3 bit flips
Detect up to 1 bit flip only
Correct any number of bit flips as long as syndrome is non-zero
questions.explanation: With d_min=3, you can guarantee correcting t where 2t+1 ≤ 3, so t=1; and detect up to d_min-1 = 2.
